question: At Grimsås in Sweden, peat production by the Finnish, state-owned company Neova has been subjected to repeated sabotage and actions by radical activist groups. In the summer of 2026, machines were blocked, ditches were filled in and seeds spread on peat surfaces. The damage caused by this sabotage could amount to around SEK 100 million.

1 The organisers have themselves stated that the actions that took place during 2026 brought together participants from Finland, Germany, Norway, France, Poland, Belgium, the United Kingdom and elsewhere.2 Previously, Swedish and Finnish activists have also carried out joint actions against the Finnish Parliament with the aim of drawing attention to Neova’s peat operations.3 In light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission consider that organised cross-border actions that result in damage to lawful commercial activity raises the issue of the EU’s collaboration against crossborder criminality?

Is the Commission prepared to facilitate information and police collaboration between the Member States affected when national authorities request it in order to combat sabotage against peat-producing enterprises?
What other measures does the Commission intend to implement to strengthen the protection for lawful strategic production from damage and production stoppages?

answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (11.11.2026) Maintaining law and order and safeguarding internal security are essential State functions pursuant to Article 4(2) of the Treaty on European Union and, thus, the responsibility of Member States. It is for the Swedish authorities to conduct investigations in the case at hand.

The EU supports Member States’ efforts to prevent and combat serious and organised crime, inter alia through the Internal Security Fund (2021–2027)1. That includes support to strengthen law enforcement cooperation, including IT and communication systems, as well as equipment, transport and facilities to tackle organised crime and terrorism.

The legislative proposal for a renewed legal framework for European Union Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation (Europol) adopted on 24 June 20262 also seeks to enhance the EU’s collective response to the growing transnational and interconnected nature of criminal threats.

In particular, it is designed to strengthen Europol as an information hub, providing Member States with a more complete criminal intelligence picture at EU level; an operational hub, supporting Member States more effectively and at an earlier stage in cross-border investigations; and a technology and innovation hub, bolstering Member States’ action with advanced capabilities, expertise and operational tools.
